value.overview: The Hook-billed Kite (Chondrohierax uncinatus) is a distinctive Neotropical raptor named for its unusually deep, strongly hooked bill. It is specialized for feeding on arboreal snails and is most often associated with forested landscapes, forest edges, and wooded wetlands. The species occurs from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America and into much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it is widespread but generally uncommon, local, and difficult to detect.
value.classification: The Hook-billed Kite belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. It is the widespread mainland species of the genus Chondrohierax; the closely related Cuban Kite is treated separately.
value.identification: This medium-sized kite has broad wings, a fairly long tail, and a distinctive oversized bill with a strongly curved upper mandible. Plumage is variable: males may be gray, females often brown, and some individuals show darker or more barred patterns. The underparts commonly have strong barring, while the tail is banded. In flight, its broad wings and slow, deliberate wingbeats can help distinguish it from smaller forest hawks. The heavy bill is the most reliable field mark.
value.rangeHabitat: The Hook-billed Kite ranges from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America, the Caribbean in limited areas, and across northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is reported on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, especially in lowlands and foothills, with occasional records reaching the Central Valley. It is generally uncommon to rare and local. Typical habitat includes humid and seasonally wet forest, woodland edges, river corridors, forest clearings, and other areas supporting arboreal snails.
value.migrationStatus: The species is primarily sedentary or locally nomadic, but some populations may make irregular or seasonal movements. In Costa Rica it has traditionally been regarded as a resident, occurring year-round on both slopes. Evidence from Kèköldi and other Central American migration-watch sites indicates that some individuals may undertake short-distance or intratropical movements, so Costa Rican records can include both local residents and moving birds.
value.breeding: The Hook-billed Kite is believed to nest in trees within or near forest, but detailed information on its breeding biology is limited. As in other raptors, a stick nest is used and the young are dependent on the adults after hatching. Breeding timing varies across its broad range and is not fully documented in Costa Rica. The species' apparent association with mature vegetation and its specialized snail diet suggest that suitable forest structure and healthy populations of arboreal snails are important during the breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: Arboreal snails make up the main food of the Hook-billed Kite, and its specialized bill is adapted for extracting them from shells. It usually forages slowly from a perch or while moving through the forest canopy, searching vegetation for snails. Small lizards, frogs, insects, and other prey may occasionally be taken, but the species is much more specialized than many other kites. Availability of tree snails probably strongly influences where it occurs and how densely it is distributed.
value.behavior: This is usually a solitary and inconspicuous raptor. It often perches quietly within forest or flies above the canopy with slow wingbeats and occasional gliding. Individuals may remain difficult to see because they spend considerable time among foliage. The species can gather at migration watchpoints in unusual numbers, although such concentrations are not typical of its everyday behavior. Its movements, social behavior, and vocal activity remain less well known than those of more familiar raptors.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered stable.
